common_name: Turn of the Century Hardy Hibiscus (Pinwheel White-to-Pink Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Turn of the Century is a Fleming Brothers hybrid whose petals fade from white at the base to dark pink at the tips, giving each open flower a distinctive pinwheel pattern.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, since hardy hibiscus is a wetland native that flowers best with steady moisture through the growing season. Turn of the Century bears 6-7 inch flowers whose white petal bases blend into dark pink tips, creating a swirled, pinwheel look that stands apart from solid-colored hardy hibiscus, and it holds an unusually long bloom season of roughly eighteen weeks from midsummer into fall. The bushy, well-branched habit keeps plants tidy without staking even under the weight of repeat flushes of bloom. Cut dead canes to the ground after hard frost and mulch the crown for winter, and be patient in spring since hardy hibiscus is often among the last perennials to break dormancy.

common_name: Old Yella Hardy Hibiscus (Creamy Yellow-White Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Old Yella is a Fleming Brothers introduction, one of the few hardy hibiscus cultivars bred for pale creamy-yellow buds opening to luminous cream-white flowers.

directions: Grow in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun with regular deep watering through summer, since hardy hibiscus naturally colonizes pond margins and ditch banks. Old Yella opens creamy yellow buds into ruffled, 10-inch, luminescent white-to-pale-yellow flowers held above broad, only lightly lobed green foliage, a softer color break from the reds and pinks that dominate most hardy hibiscus breeding. Flowering runs from late summer to frost, and the shrubby, upright habit generally needs no staking even with such large blooms. Cut the canes to the ground after frost blackens them and mulch over winter, and expect this cultivar to be slow to resprout in spring like other Hibiscus moscheutos hybrids.

common_name: Peppermint Schnapps Hardy Hibiscus (Pink with Red Peppermint-Streaked Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Peppermint Schnapps is a Bressingham hardy hibiscus hybrid with huge cotton-candy pink flowers streaked with a deep reddish-pink throat and maple-shaped foliage tinted bronze and purple.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply during dry spells to support this large-flowered hardy hibiscus through the heat of summer. Peppermint Schnapps produces 8-10 inch whitish-pink flowers dashed with streaks of deep reddish-pink radiating from the eye, set against bold, deeply cut, maple-like leaves tinted with bronze and purple that add color even before bloom begins in midsummer. The sturdy, rounded shrub habit generally stands without staking despite the dinner-plate-sized flowers, and steady bloom continues into early fall. Cut the dead stems to the ground once frost kills them back and mulch the crown, since like other hardy hibiscus this cultivar breaks dormancy later in spring than most garden perennials.
